query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The concurrent improvement of strength and ductility in high-entropy alloys can be achieved through the formation of ordered interstitial complexes and precipitation strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a disordered or ordered microstructure
generation.intervention: Introduction of interstitial elements, such as oxygen or nitrogen, and/or precipitation strengthening through heat treatment
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures, high-pressure conditions, and specific alloy compositions
generation.structural_mediator: Ordered interstitial complexes, precipitation of secondary phases, and grain refinement
generation.mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and grain boundary strengthening
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and ductility, with potential applications in high-temperature and high-stress environments
generation.baseline: Traditional high-entropy alloys with limited strength and ductility
generation.boundary: Alloy composition, processing conditions, and temperature range
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms and optimal conditions for achieving concurrent strength and ductility improvement are still unclear and require further research

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of alloy composition, processing conditions, and temperature range to evaluate the effects on strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of interstitial elements and/or precipitation strengthening does not lead to concurrent improvement of strength and ductility, the hypothesis is falsified

Question: How does the combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering affect the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of an equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy, particularly regarding the formation of secondary phases due to interstitial elements?. System: Equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (Nb: 16.67 at%, Mo: 16.67 at%, Ta: 16.67 at%, W: 16.67 at%, V: 16.67 at%, Ti: 16.67 at%) with oxygen introduction. Processing: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders (≥99.9% purity) in a high energy planetary ball mill with stainless steel balls/vial at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 13:1 under high purity argon for 40 h; followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of the 40 h milled powders in a graphite die at 1400 °C for 10 min under 30 MPa pressure, with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and cooling to 500 °C at 300 °C/min. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ on cylindrical samples (Φ3 mm × 6 mm); density measured by Archimedes' method; microstructure analyzed via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EDS. Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
